captures.q: What are the arguments in “Many and One: Division, Unity, and the Boundaries of a Corpus in Plato and Aristotle (MANY-AND-ONE-ARTICLE v2.13-AP, as submitted)” by Lee Sharks? Ground your answer in a reading of the text itself.
captures.description: THE ARTICLE READ IN ITS ORDER; ONE POSITION BROUGHT IN FROM ANOTHER NOTEBOOK: asked for the arguments of the submitted Many and One (v2.13-AP), grounded in the text, ChatGPT reads #1576 from the author's blog (mindcontrolpoems ×8) in the article's sequence: SE 34 against Prior Analytics I.31 and the four points of resolution; division terminating in identity (Metaphysics Λ.9); 'one in actuality, many in potentiality' (De anima II.2); the sophist's many accounts (Sophist 232a); collection and division, recollection (Phaedrus 265d–266c, 249c); the divided person (Republic 395, Symposium 223d); functional against biographical identity (Phaedrus 276a–277a); the six transmission functions and the function-word dispersions 0.0571 and 0.0570 as a null; and §9.4's one-maker hypothesis with its stated limits. In §9.4 it adds a third position — 'Theophrastus represents an intermediate or "first draft" position' — which the article does not contain: #1576 names Theophrastus once, in a note, and never 'first draft'; the term is the title of the archive's Theophrastus notebooks, The First Draft (#1585–#1605).

atoms.evidence: Lee Sharks’s “Many and One: Division, Unity, and the Boundaries of a Corpus in Plato and Aristotle” makes an argument
Lee Sharks’s “Many and One: Division, Unity, and the Boundaries of a Corpus in Plato and Aristotle” makes an argument
Sharks deliberately withholds the historical hypothesis until §9.4, asking the reader first to work through the philosophical texts on their own terms.
Section 8 tests whether textual and stylistic evidence can resolve the authorship question.

Sharks identifies four possible points at which an interpretation might resolve the tension: the meaning of part, the meaning of existed beforehand, the identity of the method, or the meaning of precedes.

He explicitly distinguishes the textual hypothesis from the biographical question, acknowledges that the received account remains possible, and says that papyrological, inscriptional and transmission evidence would take precedence in determining the number of historical authors.
In Sophistical Refutations 34 (183b35), Aristotle says that nothing at all existed beforehand in the inquiry he is discussing.
The account above follows the submitted article’s own sequence and distinguishes its stated textual readings from its explicitly provisional historical hypothesis.
